title: Write the film as one sentence first
rule: Before any scene, state the whole film in one sentence; if that fails, shrink the story.
why: Every practitioner source treats the one-sentence story as the gate against disconnected clips; Pixar rule 22 says the same about the essence.
how: Check: 'A <who> wants <what>, but <turn>, so <end>'. Reject stories that need two sentences for a 30-60 s film.

monofilm.idea: Add a one-sentence logline field and warn when a film over 60 s has no single turn.

title: One action per clip
rule: Give each clip exactly one subject action and at most one camera move.
why: Crowded clips distort; several guides and Sora's guide converge on one action per shot.
how: Write 'she scoops soil sideways' not 'she digs, plants, waters and smiles'; split extra verbs into the next clip.

title: Choose the shortest clip that holds the action
rule: Plan clips of about 5 s and use longer only when the action or speech needs room.
why: Shorter clips follow instructions better and leave trim handles; clips run 2-10 s.
how: Default 5 s, ceiling 8 s; two 4 s clips can beat one 8 s clip.

monofilm.idea: Prefer a shorter default when a scene's action is one beat.

title: Keep to 3-8 story beats for a short film
rule: Cap a 30-90 s film at about 3-8 beats and give each a job (setup, tension, reversal, payoff).
why: Guides give 3-7 shots for ads and six to eight 5 s clips for 30 s; extra beats dilute the payoff.
how: Label each beat: hook, setup, turn, payoff. Cut any beat that does not advance the one-sentence change.

monofilm.where: src/wizard.js READ_SYSTEM (4 to 8 beats) and SCENES_SYSTEM (3 to 8 scenes)

title: Put the key image in the first 3 seconds
rule: Open on the most compelling moment (a reaction, a reveal in motion), never a title, logo or slow establishing shot.
why: Short-form viewers decide in about 1.5-3 s; guides agree, though the percentages are unsourced.
how: Hook clip = one strong image with the problem or question visible; save place-setting for clip 2.

monofilm.idea: Tell the scene writer the first scene must show the problem, not the place.

title: One reversal per minute
rule: Use at most one twist in a film under about 60 s, and set it near the middle or late.
why: A micro-drama guide says two flips in 60 s mean neither lands; kishotenketsu also keeps one big turn at the third part.
how: Foreshadow with a visible prop in the setup clips; the twist clip changes what that prop means.

monofilm.idea: Add a check that flags a beat list with two reversals.

title: Pick the ending first and write backward
rule: Settle the final image and the feeling it should leave before writing the middle.
why: Pixar's rule 7 and a short-film guide both start from the ending; it is the hardest part to improvise.
how: Write the last state first, then choose the beats that create it.

monofilm.idea: Ask for the final image and feeling at story intake and feed it to the beat writer.

title: Carry emotion in actions, reactions and props
rule: For films with no usable dialogue, show feeling through body, reaction shots and one meaningful object.
why: Wordless storytelling relies on gestures and objects; a small prop can do the work of exposition.
how: Give the key prop one fixed look and show it in close-up at the turn.

monofilm.idea: Add a 'reaction shot' beat after the turn.

title: For small children use repetition, a gentle turn, and a return to safety
rule: In child-friendly films repeat an attempt up to three times with a small change, then resolve and return to a familiar state.
why: Children enjoy predictable patterns; the third repetition is the payoff; a critic links loops back to safety with lower anxiety. Evidence is thin.
how: Three tries, third one works; the last state matches the first state.

monofilm.idea: Offer a rule-of-three story shape for the youngest audience.

title: Restate what a later beat needs
rule: When an object or event matters in a later clip, name it again in the next scene or state, and note what carries over.
why: Each clip is a separate generation and has no memory of the earlier one.
how: Per-clip carry-over note: light direction, positions, time of day, key props.

title: Plan every shot before generating
rule: Write one sentence per shot saying what it must accomplish, then generate.
why: One author reports planned shots took 1-2 tries and improvised ones 4-7; cost of missing planning moves into the edit.
how: Beat list with place, who is present, what changes.

monofilm.where: src/wizard.js SCENES_SYSTEM and draftBeats (beats before clips)

title: Generate the hardest shot first
rule: Make the riskiest or most important clip before the easy ones.
why: If it fails, you revise the story before spending credits on the rest.
how: Order the queue by risk: the turn or the hard physical action first.

monofilm.idea: Let the take queue start with a chosen risky clip.

title: Dialogue: short lines, few per clip, one line per generation when needed
rule: Keep spoken lines short, put few in a clip, and split long exchanges across clips.
why: A 4 s clip fits one or two short exchanges; long speeches do not sync; Veo's own example uses one line per generation.
how: Quote the line, label speakers, assign each line to exactly one clip.

title: Plan the joins, not only the clips
rule: Treat the cut between clips as a design task: end mid-motion and start moving, or hand over a state.
why: Benchmarks find transitions are the weakest link in multi-clip pipelines (0.256 mean, 0.356 best).
how: Say how clip k+1 begins (continue, new angle, new place) and check it against the last frame.

title: Build the story top-down in layers
rule: Write logline, characters and places, beats, scenes, then clips, each from the layer above.
why: Hierarchical prompting kept long LLM output coherent; Re3 plan-then-write raised plot coherence by 14 points.
how: Keep each layer short enough to review; regenerate only the broken layer.

title: Check and revise LLM output in a loop
rule: After the LLM writes, review it with a second pass or a person and revise only the failing item.
why: Agentic pipelines use explore-examine-enhance loops, reranking and limited retries.
how: Validate: counts, order, impossible actions, state continuity; send the failing field back with feedback.

monofilm.idea: Add an automatic physical-possibility check on moves and states.

title: Split transformations across clips with visible stages
rule: Do not ask one short clip to show a journey, a change and a final pose; show each stage in its own clip.
why: Practitioners list this as a common cause of morphing and unusable takes.
how: Seed in soil, sprout, leaves, flower: one clip each, states frozen between.

title: Make the hook work on mute
rule: Design the first image and the payoff so they read without sound, and add captions if there is speech.
why: A large share of viewers watch muted (claims vary; unsourced).
how: Hook = visible action; narration is a bonus.

monofilm.idea: Check the hook clip has a readable visual idea without audio.

title: Trim the story, then trim again
rule: Draft the script, then cut about 30%, and give a story piece a new visual or story beat roughly every 5-7 s.
why: Vendor guidance for 30-45 s story shorts; figures are unsourced.
how: Remove any clip that restates what the last one showed.

monofilm.idea: Warn when two clips have the same beat.

title: Cliffhanger for series, resolution for children
rule: End a serial short one beat before resolution; end a young child's short with a resolved, familiar state.
why: Micro-drama guides use cliffhangers to pull the next episode; child-story sources favour predictable closure. The two goals differ.
how: Pick the ending type at intake by audience.

monofilm.idea: Add an ending-type choice (resolve, loop, cliffhanger).

title: Keep AI in service of the story
rule: Judge a finished film by narrative cohesion first, and treat visual tricks as secondary.
why: Festival coverage says best entries had story foundations; AI should not pull focus. Judging criteria include narrative cohesion.
how: Review checklist: Does the viewer know who wants what? Does each clip add a change?

monofilm.where: README 'how the studio keeps a film from drifting'
monofilm.idea: Add a story-cohesion question to the final review.
